title: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Safe Medication Practice
intro: "The right medication. The right patient. Every time." Program Outline Welcome to GNPS Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse. Nurses entering an international healthcare system must adapt to new medication charts, electronic systems, prescribing conventions, controlled-drug processes and professional standards. They are expected to explain the reasoning behind medication decisions, identify high-risk situations and communicate concerns clearly. This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations. It strengthens clinical pharmacology, high-risk medication management, patient assessment, medication reconciliation, interprofessional communication and evidence-informed decision-making. What You Will Learn Apply internationally recognised medication-safety principles Interpret medication orders and electronic medication records safely Use clinical reasoning before, during and after medication administration Manage high-risk medicines and medicines requiring independent checks Recognise and respond to adverse drug reactions and interactions Participate in medication reconciliation and transitions of care Communicate medication concerns using structured professional communication Provide culturally responsive medication education Report medication incidents and near misses appropriately Why This Learning Matters International medication practice requires more than following a chart. Nurses must integrate the order with the patient's current condition, allergies, pathology results, other medicines and treatment goals. Safe international practice combines technical competence with clinical judgement and professional accountability. Your Learning Goal By completing Level 2, you should be able to manage medicines safely within international healthcare environments, recognise complex medication risks and communicate confidently with patients and multidisciplinary teams.

content.text: International healthcare systems use different charts, formularies, electronic records and controlled-drug procedures. Although local processes vary, safe practice is built on consistent identification, allergy checking, clinical assessment, documentation and communication. An IQN must learn the local system before practising independently.
Learning outcomes
Relate local medication policy to broader safety principles Interpret paper and electronic medication orders safely
Adapt to unfamiliar medication systems Practise within professional and organisational requirements

Local Policy and Professional Standards Nurses should understand who may prescribe, administer, check, store and dispose of medicines in their workplace. Local policy describes the required process, while professional standards define accountability, competence and the duty to protect patients.

Medication Orders A valid order should identify the patient, medicine, dose, route, timing and prescriber. Abbreviations, incomplete instructions, unclear decimals and verbal orders can create risk. Uncertainty must be clarified before administration.

Electronic Medication Systems Electronic medication administration records can improve allergy alerts, scheduling and traceability. They can also introduce risks such as selecting the wrong patient, copying outdated information, alert fatigue or assuming that the system has checked everything.

Safe Transition IQNs should request orientation to local medicines, storage systems, infusion devices, controlled-drug processes and independent-check requirements. Previous experience is valuable but does not replace local competence assessment.

During orientation in an overseas hospital, an IQN sees that insulin is prescribed and documented electronically using unfamiliar abbreviations. Rather than relying on previous practice, the nurse reviews the local policy, confirms the intended insulin and dose with the prescriber and completes supervised administration.
Key learning points
Learn the medication systems used in your workplace Clarify incomplete or ambiguous orders
Do not rely only on electronic alerts Seek supervision until local competence is confirmed

Some medicines have a greater potential to cause serious harm if used incorrectly. Internationally qualified nurses must combine pharmacological knowledge with current patient assessment, pathology results and monitoring requirements.
Learning outcomes
Recognise common high-risk medication groups Apply additional safeguards to high-risk medicines
Use clinical data to support medication decisions Respond to abnormal findings before administration

High-Risk Medicines High-risk groups commonly include insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated electrolytes, sedatives, chemotherapy and some intravenous medicines. These medicines may require restricted storage, standard concentrations, independent checks and closer monitoring.

Clinical Assessment The nurse should connect the medication order with the patient's current condition. Blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, blood glucose, renal function, electrolyte levels, swallowing ability and pain score may influence whether a dose is appropriate.

Independent Double Checks A meaningful independent check requires each clinician to verify the order, patient, medicine, calculation and relevant assessment separately before comparing results. Simply watching another person prepare the medicine is not an independent check.

Therapeutic Monitoring Some medicines require drug levels, coagulation results, blood glucose, ECG monitoring or renal and liver tests. The nurse should know which findings require withholding a dose and seeking review according to policy.

A patient receiving an anticoagulant has new bruising and a significantly abnormal coagulation result. The nurse withholds the dose according to policy, assesses for bleeding, informs the medical team and documents the findings. The medicine is not administered simply because it appears on the chart.
Key learning points
Treat high-risk medicines with additional safeguards Link every dose to the patient's current assessment
Perform independent checks independently Escalate abnormal results before administration

sections.title: Medication Reconciliation, Communication and Incident Management

content.text: Medication harm often occurs when patients move between home, emergency care, hospital wards, aged care and community services. Accurate medication reconciliation and clear communication protect patients during these transitions.
Learning outcomes
Explain the purpose of medication reconciliation Identify discrepancies in medication histories
Communicate medication concerns effectively Manage medication incidents and near misses professionally

Medication Reconciliation Reconciliation compares the medicines a patient was actually taking with current orders. It includes prescription medicines, non-prescription products, supplements, allergies and recent changes. Differences should be identified, clarified and documented.

Transitions of Care Admission, transfer and discharge are high-risk periods. Accurate lists, clear instructions and communication with community providers reduce omitted medicines, duplication and confusion.

Structured Communication ISBAR or another approved framework helps communicate medication concerns clearly. The nurse should state the patient, medicine, current problem, relevant findings and the action required.

Incident Management The patient should be assessed first. The appropriate clinician and senior nurse should be notified, treatment initiated and documentation completed. Incident reports should record facts and contributing conditions rather than blame.

A patient admitted after a fall reports taking a blood thinner at home, but it is absent from the admission chart. The nurse confirms the medicine with the patient, pharmacy and previous records, informs the prescriber and ensures the discrepancy is resolved before the next dose is due.
Key learning points
Reconcile medicines at every transition Include non-prescription and complementary medicines
Communicate discrepancies promptly Use incident reporting to support learning

sections.title: Person-Centred Medication Education and Shared Decision-Making

content.text: Medication safety improves when patients understand and participate in treatment decisions. International nurses care for people with different languages, beliefs, health literacy and access to medicines. Education should be individualised without making assumptions.
Learning outcomes
Assess medication-related learning needs Provide culturally responsive medication education
Use shared decision-making and teach-back Support safe self-management and adherence

Health Literacy Patients may have difficulty understanding labels, schedules or risk information even when they speak the same language as the clinician. Plain language, visual aids, demonstration and written plans can reduce confusion.

Cultural and Personal Beliefs Beliefs about illness, fasting, traditional medicines or dependence may influence medication use. The nurse should ask respectfully, explore concerns and coordinate safe options with the healthcare team.
Shared Decision-Making Patients should understand available options, benefits and risks and have an opportunity to express preferences. Shared decisions improve trust and may strengthen adherence.

Teach-Back and Self-Management Teach-back asks the patient to explain how they will use the medicine. Education should also address storage, missed doses, monitoring, driving, pregnancy, alcohol and when to seek help where relevant.

A patient with limited English is discharged with insulin. The nurse arranges a professional interpreter, demonstrates the device, provides a simple written schedule and asks the patient to demonstrate the injection and explain signs of low blood glucose. A technique error is corrected before discharge.
Key learning points
Adapt education to language and health literacy Ask about beliefs and complementary medicines
Invite patients to participate in decisions Use teach-back and demonstration to confirm understanding

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 3 - Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to apply international medication standards, manage high-risk medicines, reconcile medication histories and support patients through clear education and shared decision-making. You are now prepared to progress to Level 3, where the focus moves from safe individual practice to leadership, governance and medication-system improvement.
